stem: The pan-Islamic movement (1919-24) launched by Indian Muslims to pressurise the British to preserve the Ottoman Caliph's authority after World War I, which Gandhi controversially yoked to the Non-Cooperation Movement to build Hindu-Muslim unity, was the:
explanation: The Khilafat Movement, led by the Ali Brothers (Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali), protested the harsh Treaty of Sèvres terms imposed on the Ottoman Caliph; Gandhi linked it to Non-Cooperation to unite Hindus and Muslims against British rule, though the alliance collapsed after Chauri Chaura (1922).

stem: Founded by Chittaranjan Das and Motilal Nehru in 1923, this party's strategy was to contest and enter the newly-created legislative councils (under the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms) in order to obstruct government business from within, rather than boycott elections entirely. This party was the:
explanation: The Swaraj Party emerged after the suspension of Non-Cooperation (1922) when Congress split over council entry; C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru favoured a 'council-entry' strategy of obstructionism from within legislatures, distinct from 'no-changers' who opposed council entry.

section: Social Studies · Ch — Modern India & National Movement
subject: Social Studies
stem: The 1878 law enacted by Viceroy Lord Lytton that empowered the government to confiscate the press and equipment of newspapers publishing material deemed seditious, targeting Indian-language (vernacular) newspapers while exempting English-language papers, was the:
explanation: The Vernacular Press Act (1878), dubbed the 'gagging act', discriminated against Indian-language newspapers by allowing pre-censorship and confiscation without judicial recourse — it was repealed in 1882 under Viceroy Lord Ripon following widespread protest.

section: Social Studies · Ch — Modern India & National Movement
subject: Social Studies
stem: The reformist Hindu organisation founded by Swami Dayananda Saraswati in 1875, which advocated a return to the authority of the Vedas, opposed idol worship, and campaigned against child marriage, was the:
explanation: Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj (1875) on the slogan 'Back to the Vedas', rejecting idol worship, caste rigidity, and untouchability — distinct from Raja Ram Mohan Roy's Brahmo Samaj (1828), which was more accommodating of Western rationalist influence.

section: Social Studies · Ch — Modern India & National Movement
subject: Social Studies
stem: Founded in Bombay in 1867 by Atmaram Pandurang and later closely associated with Justice Mahadev Govind Ranade, this socio-religious reform society worked within the Bombay Presidency for widow remarriage and women's education, broadly sharing the Brahmo Samaj's monotheistic ideals. It was the:
explanation: The Prarthana Samaj (1867), influenced by the Brahmo Samaj, focused its reform activity on the Bombay Presidency — M.G. Ranade and R.G. Bhandarkar were prominent members championing widow remarriage and female education, distinct from Jyotiba Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj which focused on anti-caste mobilisation.
